title: What Happened When Neuroscientists Started a Mouse Fight Club - Nautilus
gist: Teaser on a Princeton neuroscience study published in Nature. Male lab mice were split into fighters, spectators and novices for an eight-day regimen to test how watching fights changes behavior; the subtitle says their brain activity shifted. Results are cut off.

insights.claim: Princeton neuroscientists set up a 'sparring camp' for lab mice, published in Nature, to find out how watching a fight influences a mouse's behavior.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Research on whether watching aggression changes the brain is relevant to debates about violent media and social learning.
insights.quote: to find out how watching a fight influenced their behavior
insights.locator: The first rule of fight club

insights.claim: The design split male mice into three groups for eight days: fighters sparred against weaker opponents, spectators watched two other mice fight, and novices played with a mouse-shaped stuffed toy as a control.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: This three-arm design separates the effect of watching a fight from the effect of fighting.
insights.quote: The fighters sparred against a weaker opponent, the spectators watched two other mice fight

insights.claim: The article reports that the brain activity of the mice shifted after the fight-club regimen, but the excerpt does not give the specific findings.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Watch the full Nature paper for whether spectators acquire neural signatures similar to fighters'.
